body:
Why semiconductors are important

A smartphone can process information, store photographs, receive wireless signals and control its battery because it contains electronic components made using semiconductor materials. Similar components are found in computers, vehicles, medical equipment, industrial machines, communication networks and electricity-control systems.

A semiconductor is a material whose electrical conductivity can be controlled by factors such as the addition of selected impurities, temperature, light and applied electric fields. This ability to control the movement of electric charge makes semiconductors particularly suitable for electronic devices.

Conductors, insulators and semiconductors

Electrical conductivity describes how readily a material permits electric current to flow. In metals such as copper, many electrons can move through the material, so copper is widely used for electrical connections. Materials such as rubber and glass ordinarily resist the flow of electric current and are useful as insulators.

Semiconductors behave differently. Their conductivity is ordinarily lower than that of good metallic conductors but can be changed substantially under suitable conditions. The important characteristic is controllable conductivity, not a fixed conductivity exactly halfway between that of a conductor and an insulator.

Material categoryTypical exampleElectrical behaviour
ConductorCopperAllows current to flow readily.
InsulatorRubberStrongly resists current under ordinary conditions.
SemiconductorSiliconConductivity can be controlled for electronic functions.

Silicon is the most widely used semiconductor material in conventional integrated circuits. Germanium is another elemental semiconductor. Silicon carbide (SiC) and gallium nitride (GaN) are compound semiconductors used in selected applications, including power-electronic devices. Different semiconductor materials are chosen according to the intended device and operating requirements.

How a semiconductor becomes useful in a circuit

Electrons, holes and doping

Electric current involves the movement of electric charge. In a semiconductor, current can be carried by mobile electrons and by holes. A hole represents the absence of an electron in a position that can otherwise be occupied. When neighbouring electrons move into available positions, the hole behaves as though a positive charge carrier is moving through the material.

Doping is the deliberate introduction of small quantities of suitable impurity atoms into a semiconductor to change its electrical properties. For example, adding phosphorus to silicon supplies additional electrons, while adding boron creates additional holes.

TypeTypical silicon dopantMajority charge carrier
n-type semiconductorPhosphorusElectrons
p-type semiconductorBoronHoles

The letters n and p identify the majority charge carriers. They do not mean that an entire piece of n-type semiconductor has a net negative charge or that an entire piece of p-type semiconductor has a net positive charge. Ordinary doped semiconductor material remains electrically neutral overall.

The p-n junction and semiconductor diode

When p-type and n-type semiconductor regions meet, they form a p-n junction. Near their boundary, a region with relatively few mobile charge carriers develops. This creates a barrier to the movement of additional charge carriers.

A basic semiconductor diode uses this junction to permit substantial current mainly in 1 direction. Under forward bias, with the positive supply connected to the p-side and the negative supply to the n-side, the barrier is reduced and current can flow more readily. Under reverse bias, the barrier is increased and current is normally very small. This is the basic principle of rectification, which is used to convert alternating current into direct current.

Transistors and integrated circuits

A transistor is a semiconductor device that can act as an electronic switch or amplify an electrical signal. When transistors act as switches, they help electronic circuits represent and process digital information. When used for amplification, they allow a small input signal to control a larger output signal.

An integrated circuit (IC) contains many electronic components, especially transistors, fabricated together on a small semiconductor chip. Different ICs perform different functions:

  • Processor: carries out instructions and calculations.
  • Memory chip: stores data or instructions.
  • Microcontroller: combines processing, memory and input-output functions to control equipment.
  • Power-management chip: regulates or controls electrical power supplied to electronic equipment.

A printed circuit board (PCB) is different from a semiconductor chip. It is the board on which chips and other components are mounted and electrically connected. A finished electronic product often contains several different chips on 1 or more PCBs.

Prelims focus

  • Silicon is the principal semiconductor material used in conventional integrated circuits.
  • Doping changes semiconductor conductivity by introducing suitable impurities.
  • n-type material has electrons as majority carriers; p-type material has holes as majority carriers.
  • A p-n junction is the basis of a conventional semiconductor diode.
  • A transistor can perform switching or amplification.
  • Trap: A semiconductor chip and a printed circuit board are not the same component.

[NCERT, Science, Class 6, Chapter 12, Electricity and Circuits, printed pp. 116–121, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 4, Materials: Metals and Non-Metals, printed pp. 44–46, 2018–19 printing; OpenStax, University Physics Volume 3, Sections 9.6, Semiconductors and Doping, and 9.7, Semiconductor Devices; Semiconductor Industry Association, Introduction to Semiconductors, semiconductor applications; online sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

title: Semiconductors: Materials That Make Modern Electronics Possible

body:
Why chip production involves several stages

A semiconductor chip is not made simply by cutting a small piece of silicon and connecting wires to it. The electronic functions must first be designed, and microscopic patterns must then be formed within and on the surface of semiconductor material.

The semiconductor value chain therefore separates the intellectual work of chip design from the industrial work of fabrication. It also includes subsequent packaging, testing and integration into electronic products.

Chip design

Chip design begins with identifying the function the chip must perform. A designer of a microcontroller, for example, must determine how it will process information, store instructions and communicate with sensors or other devices.

Designers then prepare the electronic logic and physical arrangement of the components. They use Electronic Design Automation (EDA) software to develop, simulate, check and refine the design before it is sent for manufacturing. Verification at this stage helps detect problems before the more expensive fabrication process begins.

Design and manufacturing are related but separate activities. A company may possess considerable expertise in designing semiconductor devices without operating a wafer-fabrication factory.

Fabless companies, foundries and integrated manufacturers

Business modelMain responsibilityManufacturing arrangement
Fabless semiconductor companyDesigns semiconductor chips.Normally contracts a foundry to fabricate them.
Semiconductor foundryFabricates chips using supplied designs.Operates wafer-fabrication facilities.
Integrated Device Manufacturer (IDM)Designs and manufactures semiconductor devices.Operates its own manufacturing facilities, although some work may be outsourced.

The distinction concerns the company's role in the value chain. A fabless company does not become a fabrication plant merely because its chip design is manufactured elsewhere.

How silicon wafers are fabricated

A semiconductor fabrication facility is commonly called a fab. Most conventional integrated circuits begin with highly purified silicon derived from silica-containing raw materials. The silicon is formed into a crystal, sliced into thin circular wafers and prepared with a very smooth surface.

A single silicon wafer contains locations for many individual chips. The circuits are formed through repeated manufacturing operations, rather than by drawing or printing a complete finished circuit in 1 step.

Basic fabrication stages

  1. Wafer preparation: High-purity semiconductor material is prepared as a suitable wafer.
  2. Deposition: Thin layers of selected materials are added to the wafer.
  3. Photolithography: Light is used with a patterned template and light-sensitive material to transfer microscopic circuit patterns.
  4. Etching: Selected material is removed to produce the required patterns.
  5. Doping: Suitable impurities are introduced into selected semiconductor regions to control their electrical properties.
  6. Repeated layer formation: Additional semiconductor, conducting and insulating regions are produced to complete the integrated circuits.
  7. Inspection and testing: The fabricated patterns and electrical functions are checked before the individual chips proceed to later stages.

The listed operations describe the main ideas, not a fixed sequence followed only once. Actual fabrication uses many repeated, carefully controlled operations. Manufacturing is performed in a cleanroom, where airborne particles and environmental conditions are controlled because contamination can damage extremely small circuit features.

Semiconductor fabs and display fabs

A semiconductor fab makes semiconductor devices such as integrated circuits. A display fab manufactures display panels or components used in screens. The 2 industries may share some manufacturing technologies, but a display-fabrication project should not automatically be counted as a silicon integrated-circuit wafer fab.

The distinction matters when comparing industrial investment announcements. A proposal for a semiconductor design centre, an IC fabrication plant, a display manufacturing facility or a packaging plant represents a different activity.

Prelims focus

  • EDA means Electronic Design Automation and is used in chip design and verification.
  • A fabless company designs chips without operating its own wafer fab.
  • A foundry manufactures semiconductor chips.
  • Photolithography transfers microscopic patterns using light-sensitive material.
  • Fabrication forms circuits on semiconductor wafers; it is different from packaging finished dies.
  • Trap: A display fab is not necessarily an integrated-circuit wafer fab.

[Semiconductor Industry Association, How Are Semiconductors Made?, Stages 2 and 3, chip design and front-end manufacturing; Semiconductor Industry Association, Introduction to Semiconductors, Primer on the Industry Ecosystem; ASML, How Microchips Are Made, Deposition, Lithography, Etching and Repeat as Needed sections; Press Information Bureau, India Building Semiconductor Future, 17 September 2026, semiconductor value-chain overview; online sources consulted 5 November 2026.]

title: Chip Design and Semiconductor Fabrication: From an Idea to a Wafer

body:
What happens after wafer fabrication?

After fabrication, a silicon wafer contains many individual circuit regions. These regions must be checked, separated and prepared for connection to the outside world. The resulting component must also be able to withstand normal handling and operating conditions.

An individual piece of fabricated semiconductor material containing a circuit is called a die. A wafer ordinarily contains many dies, while a package can contain 1 or more dies, depending on its design.

Back-end manufacturing stages

  1. Wafer testing: Electrical measurements help identify dies that meet requirements before further processing.
  2. Dicing: The wafer is separated into individual dies.
  3. Die attachment: A die is fixed to a suitable base or substrate.
  4. Electrical interconnection: Connections are formed between the die and the package terminals.
  5. Packaging: The die and its connections are protected by a suitable package.
  6. Final testing and marking: The finished component is checked and identified before being supplied for use.

Packaging has practical functions. It protects the fragile die, provides electrical connections to other equipment and helps manage heat generated during operation. Testing checks whether the device performs correctly and meets its specified requirements.

ATMP and OSAT: similar work, different emphasis

ATMP stands for Assembly, Testing, Marking and Packaging. It describes a set of semiconductor manufacturing activities performed after wafer fabrication.

OSAT stands for Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test. It commonly refers to a business that provides assembly and testing services to other semiconductor companies. OSAT operations can include packaging and related processes.

ATMP describes activities; OSAT describes an outsourced service model. Both relate mainly to back-end manufacturing. Neither term, by itself, means that the company fabricates silicon integrated circuits on wafers.

After testing, packaged semiconductor components can be mounted on printed circuit boards together with resistors, capacitors, connectors and other parts. This is part of broader electronics manufacturing and produces functional boards or systems.

Materials, machinery and other essential inputs

A semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem depends on more than silicon. Different stages need different materials, machines, services and technical skills.

InputTypical useWhy it matters
High-purity silicon wafersBase material for many semiconductor devices.Impurities and defects can affect performance.
Specialty chemicals and gasesCleaning, deposition, etching and other fabrication steps.Manufacturing requires controlled chemical purity.
Photomasks and photoresistTransfer of microscopic circuit patterns.They help form the intended patterns.
Manufacturing and inspection equipmentFabrication, measurement and defect detection.Reliable processing depends on precise equipment.
Packaging materials and substratesProtection and electrical connection of dies.They make chips suitable for integration into products.

Other requirements include skilled workers, dependable electricity, suitable water supply, cleanrooms, logistics, engineering services and waste-management systems. These requirements influence where semiconductor facilities can operate successfully.

Why semiconductor supply chains are international

The production of a chip often involves companies in several countries. A design may be produced in 1 location, fabricated in another, packaged and tested elsewhere, and finally assembled into an electronic product in a further location.

This division of work allows companies to specialise, but it also creates dependencies. A shortage of a particular chemical, manufacturing machine, wafer or packaging service can delay production. Difficulties in transport, trade restrictions, natural disasters or interruptions in utilities may affect the wider electronics industry.

A country seeking a stronger semiconductor industry therefore needs capabilities across the value chain: design, materials, equipment, fabrication, packaging, testing, skills and supporting infrastructure. Building only 1 stage does not automatically remove dependence on the remaining stages.

Why environmental management matters

Semiconductor production can require substantial electricity, ultrapure water and specialised chemicals. The environmental impact depends on the manufacturing process and the quality of resource management. Recycling, efficient water use, energy management and safe chemical treatment are therefore important considerations. A domestic chip industry may strengthen supply security, but it does not automatically have a low environmental impact.

Prelims focus

  • A wafer normally contains many semiconductor dies.
  • Dicing separates individual dies from a fabricated wafer.
  • ATMP means Assembly, Testing, Marking and Packaging.
  • OSAT means Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test.
  • Packaging provides protection, electrical connections and support for heat management.
  • Trap: An operating packaging or testing plant is not proof that a complete wafer-fabrication plant is operational.

[Semiconductor Industry Association, How Are Semiconductors Made?, Stage 4, Back-End Manufacturing, Dicing through Testing; Semiconductor Industry Association, Introduction to Semiconductors, supply-chain and manufacturing overview; ASML, How Microchips Are Made, Processed Wafer section; Press Information Bureau, India Building Semiconductor Future, 17 September 2026, manufacturing materials and packaging; online sources consulted 5 November 2026.]
